stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Marisol Etxeberria's 2019 memoir Counting Owls.

For my first season on the survey crew, I treated the beech forest as a list: forty transects, so many nests, so many pellets weighed and bagged. <u>By August, though, I had begun to notice that the owls hunted where the voles fed, and the voles fed where the beechnuts fell.</u> The list, I realized, had always been a web; I had simply been reading it one strand at a time.
choices: It explains why the survey crew moved its transects to the areas where beechnuts fell.
It marks the start of a change in how the narrator sees the forest, from separate counts to linked relationships.
It contrasts the narrator's survey methods with the methods of more experienced members of the crew.
It summarizes the data on nests and pellets that the narrator gathered during her first season.
explanation: Read the sentences on either side of the underlined line. Before it, the narrator treats the forest as "a list" of separate counts. After it, she says the list "had always been a web." The underlined line, which opens with "though," is where she first notices that owls, voles, and beechnuts are linked. Its job is to mark the start of that change in how she sees the forest.

A.why: You made up a result the text never mentions. Nothing says the crew moved its transects. The narrator only notices a pattern, and you can't point to any words that show the survey changed.

C.why: You brought in people the text never mentions. No experienced crew members appear, and no one's methods are compared. The only contrast is between how the narrator saw the forest before and how she sees it now.

D.why: You picked up on the survey details from the first sentence and gave them to the wrong line. The underlined sentence doesn't sum up any data. It describes a new observation that turns the narrator away from simply counting.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Rejn's 2008 novel The Low Country. Pieter, a hydrologist, has returned to the farm where he grew up.

His father had always read the river by its color, calling it "tea" in spring and "slate" after the autumn rains. Pieter now carried a turbidity meter that reported the same water in precise units, accurate to a decimal place. <u>Standing on the bank beside the old man, he found that he could not say which of them actually knew the river better.</u>
choices: It reveals that Pieter has decided his meter's readings are more reliable than his father's names.
It describes an argument in which Pieter and his father disagree about how to measure the river.
It conveys Pieter's uncertainty about whether his instrument gives him a deeper knowledge than his father's.
It shifts the focus from the river to the farm that Pieter left behind as a young man.
explanation: The first two sentences set two ways of knowing the river side by side: the father's color names and Pieter's precise meter. The underlined line then says Pieter "could not say which of them actually knew the river better." Its job is to show that he is unsure whether his scientific measurement really tells him more than his father's way of reading the water.

A.why: You turned the line around. Pieter "could not say" which way of knowing is better, so he has not decided that his meter wins. The sentence expresses doubt, not a conclusion.

B.why: You made up a conversation. Pieter and his father stand side by side, but no one speaks or disagrees. The comparison happens only in Pieter's mind, and you can't point to any words that show an argument.

D.why: You latched onto the background about the farm in the introduction. The underlined line never mentions the farm. It stays on the river and on the two ways of knowing it.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Adaeze Okafor's 2021 memoir Weighed Portions, about her years as a hospital dietitian.

For a decade I had believed what my training taught: that a patient who understood the numbers would eat accordingly. I wrote meal plans to the gram and explained each one with care. <u>Then Mrs. Halvorsen handed back her plan, folded neatly into a paper boat, and asked whether I had ever cooked for anyone I loved.</u>
choices: It presents an encounter that calls into question a belief the narrator had long held about her work.
It shows that Mrs. Halvorsen enjoyed making paper crafts to pass the time during her hospital stay.
It describes a family recipe that Mrs. Halvorsen offered to share with the narrator after her meal.
It summarizes the detailed meal plans the narrator had written for patients over the previous decade.
explanation: The first sentence states something the narrator "had believed" for a decade: if patients understand the numbers, they will eat accordingly. The word "Then" introduces a patient who folds the plan into a boat and asks about cooking for loved ones. That response suggests numbers aren't enough. So the underlined line presents a moment that challenges the narrator's long-held belief.

B.why: You read the paper boat literally, as a hobby. Folding the plan into a boat is a way of handing it back and setting it aside. It says nothing about how Mrs. Halvorsen passes her time.

C.why: You added something the text never shows. Mrs. Halvorsen asks a question about cooking, but she offers no recipe. You can't point to any words that support this choice.

D.why: You gave the second sentence's job to the underlined line. The earlier sentences describe the meal plans. The underlined line doesn't sum them up. It brings in a patient's reaction that challenges them.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ines Valcourt's 2015 novel Pressure Systems. Odile works as a forecaster at a small coastal weather station.

The computer models agreed: the storm would turn north and spare the harbor. Odile signed off on the forecast at noon. <u>All afternoon, though, she kept walking to the window to watch the gulls, which had stopped circling the boats and were flying inland in long, low lines.</u>
choices: It shows that Odile is fully confident the storm will turn north and leave the harbor alone.
It describes a conversation in which Odile warns the local fishers to bring in their boats.
It establishes that the weather station where Odile works sits close to a busy harbor.
It suggests that Odile has doubts about the forecast she approved earlier in the day.
explanation: The sentence before the underlined line says Odile approved a forecast that the storm would miss the harbor. The underlined line starts with "though" and shows her returning to the window again and again to watch gulls flee inland. Her repeated checking, set against the official forecast, suggests she isn't sure the forecast is right.

A.why: You missed the contrast that "though" sets up. Odile keeps going back to watch the gulls, which shows unease, not confidence. Confidence belongs to the models in the first sentence, not to Odile in this line.

B.why: You made up a conversation. Odile watches from a window and speaks to no one. Nothing in the text shows her warning anyone.

C.why: You chose a background detail the line happens to suggest, not the line's job in the passage. You could write this choice after reading only the underlined sentence. Its real role comes from how it pushes against the forecast in the sentences before it.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Rafael Duarte's 2012 memoir The Hiring Hall, about growing up near a shipyard.

The economists who toured the yard spoke of wages as a price, set wherever the supply of welders met the demand for them. My uncle, who had welded hulls for thirty years, spoke of wages differently. <u>To him, every raise the union won was a door held open for the men behind him in line.</u>
choices: It describes the uncle's habit of holding doors open for coworkers as they entered the hiring hall.
It shows that the uncle agreed with the economists that wages are set by supply and demand.
It explains the uncle's view that wages carry an obligation to other workers, unlike a market price.
It lists the specific raises that the union won during the uncle's thirty years at the shipyard.
explanation: The text first gives the economists' view of wages as a market price. Then it says the uncle "spoke of wages differently." The underlined line spells out that difference with an image: each raise is "a door held open" for the workers who come after him. Its job is to explain the uncle's view that wages are about what workers owe one another, not just a price.

A.why: You took a figure of speech as a physical fact. The "door held open" is a metaphor for how one raise helps later workers. It doesn't describe the uncle actually holding doors.

B.why: You reversed the contrast. The text says the uncle "spoke of wages differently" from the economists. The underlined line describes how his view differs from theirs, not how it matches.

D.why: You added details the text never gives. The line mentions "every raise" in general, but it names no amounts and no list. You can't point to any specific raises in the passage.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Mara Lindqvist's 2019 memoir about her years surveying wetlands.

During my first summer at the marsh, I counted herons the way I had been trained: one tally mark per bird, nothing more. Dr. Okafor, however, never seemed to count at all. She would stand at the edge of the reeds for an hour, watching a single heron stalk the shallows, and return with pages of notes on how it moved. I had a number; she had a bird.
choices: To recount a disagreement between the narrator and Dr. Okafor about the best way to count herons
To contrast the narrator's narrow way of observing the marsh with Dr. Okafor's more attentive one
To explain why the number of herons living in the marsh had changed over the summer
To describe the way herons move through shallow water while they search for food
explanation: The 'however' sets the narrator's tally marks against Dr. Okafor's hour of watching one bird, and the last line, 'I had a number; she had a bird,' sums up the contrast. The text's purpose is to set the narrator's thin, number-only way of observing against her mentor's close attention.

A.why: You added a conversation the text never shows. The two approaches are set side by side, but nobody argues about them. Check that you can point to the words that support a choice.

C.why: You assumed the counting was building toward a finding about the heron population. The text never says anything about the numbers going up or down.

D.why: You picked up a detail, Dr. Okafor's notes on how a heron moves, and treated it as the point. The heron's movement only serves the contrast between the two observers. The text never actually describes it.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Eberle's 2008 memoir of his career as an archaeologist.

On my first dig, I believed the job was to find things: a coin, a blade, anything that would photograph well. Then, in the third week, the director had me spend a whole day brushing the floor of an empty hut. There was nothing in it but packed earth and a darker stain where a hearth had been. By evening I understood that the stain was the find: someone had kept warm there for years.
choices: To argue that hearths are the most valuable kind of evidence an archaeological site can offer
To express the narrator's resentment at being given dull work by the director of the dig
To explain how the narrator identified the remains of an old fire by the color of the soil
To show how one experience changed the narrator's sense of what counts as a discovery
explanation: The text opens with what the narrator 'believed' (finds are objects that photograph well) and turns on 'Then' to a day spent on an empty floor. It ends with him seeing that a stain of daily life 'was the find.' Its purpose is to show his idea of discovery changing.

A.why: You turned one personal realization into a general ranking of evidence. The narrator never says hearths are worth more than anything else.

B.why: You read a feeling into the text that it never states. The brushing is where he learns something, and nothing in the text shows him complaining about it.

C.why: You took the stain literally, as a technical clue, when it marks a shift in how he thinks. This is the content trap: it is true that the stain is darker, but that isn't why the passage was written.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Inês Carvalho's 2015 memoir about collecting folktales in rural Portugal.

I arrived with a recorder and a list of the stories I hoped to hear. My first storyteller, an old miller named Duarte, glanced at the list and set it face down on the table. He then told me a tale I had never seen in any collection, and another after that, until the tape ran out. I did not take the list out again.
choices: To show the narrator learning that her storytellers, not her planned list, should guide her work
To suggest that Duarte distrusted outsiders who came to his village to record local stories
To explain that the narrator's recording equipment failed during her very first interview
To identify the folktales that Duarte considered most important to the history of his village
explanation: Duarte turns the list face down and then tells stories the narrator had never come across. Her closing line, 'I did not take the list out again,' shows she has learned to let her storytellers lead instead of her own expectations.

B.why: You read distrust into his gesture. Duarte goes on to tell story after story, which is the opposite of shutting an outsider out.

C.why: You took 'until the tape ran out' as a breakdown. It means he had so many stories that the tape filled up, so it shows abundance, not a failure.

D.why: You invented a list of topics. The text never names any of Duarte's tales or says which ones he valued most.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Hana Mori's 2021 novel. Emiko, a textile historian, is examining a quilt in a museum archive.

Emiko had catalogued hundreds of quilts, each by its pattern, its dyes, its decade. This one resisted. Its squares had been cut from at least six different garments, among them a child's smock, a man's work shirt, and the faded hem of a wedding dress, and the seams no longer looked to her like stitching but like a family held together by hand.
choices: To explain the sewing technique used to join squares cut from several different garments
To describe how Emiko worked out the decade in which the quilt had most likely been made
To show Emiko coming to see the quilt as a record of lives rather than an item to classify
To suggest that Emiko intends to find the descendants of the family who made the quilt
explanation: First Emiko's usual routine is laid out: pattern, dyes, decade. Then 'This one resisted,' and the seams turn into 'a family held together by hand.' The text's purpose is to show the quilt meaning more to her than its physical features do.

A.why: You read the seams literally, as needlework. The text turns them into a figure of speech for a family, and it never describes how the squares were sewn.

B.why: You missed 'This one resisted.' This quilt is the one Emiko can't sort by pattern, dyes, and decade the way she usually does.

D.why: You gave Emiko a plan the text never mentions. Nothing is said about what she does next.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Rafael Soto's 2017 memoir about his work as a materials scientist.

In graduate school, I was taught that every crack in a sample was a failure, something to log and discard. My grandmother, who mended pottery, would have disagreed. She filled the breaks in her bowls with resin dusted with gold, so the repaired lines shone brighter than the clay around them. Years later, designing a polymer that seals its own fractures, I kept thinking of those bright seams.
choices: To describe the materials the narrator's grandmother used when she repaired her broken bowls
To show how a memory of his grandmother's craft shaped the narrator's view of damage in his work
To argue that self-sealing polymers are stronger than pottery that has been repaired with gold
To recount an argument the narrator had with his grandmother about his graduate training
explanation: The text sets what he was taught (cracks are failures) against his grandmother's mending, which made breaks the brightest part of a bowl. It ends with him thinking of 'those bright seams' while he designs a material that heals its own cracks. Its purpose is to show how that memory changed the way he sees damage.

A.why: This is the content trap. Resin and gold really are in the text, but they serve as an image that changes how the narrator thinks. Describing them isn't the point of the passage.

C.why: You made up a comparison. The text never measures or compares the strength of the polymer and the bowls.

D.why: You read 'would have disagreed' as a real argument. The phrase is hypothetical, so no conversation between them takes place in the text.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Marisol Okafor's 2017 memoir about her years as a reef surveyor.

For my first season I counted parrotfish the way I had been taught, as tally marks on a slate. Then, one gray morning off the outer reef, I watched a single parrotfish grind a dead coral branch into a plume of white sand that drifted toward the beach I had walked at dawn. After that, I could never again see the fish as a number; each one was a small mill making the shore.
choices: To explain the procedure that reef surveyors follow when counting parrotfish on a slate
To describe how one observation changed the narrator's view of parrotfish from tallies to shore builders
To argue that slate counts are an unreliable method that reef surveyors should stop using
To show that parrotfish harm reefs by grinding living coral into sand that washes away
explanation: The text moves from how the narrator first saw parrotfish ("tally marks on a slate") to one morning that changed that view ("After that, I could never again see the fish as a number"). The closing image of each fish as "a small mill making the shore" is figurative. It means the fish build the beach. So the text's purpose is to describe how one observation changed the narrator's understanding, which is what B says.

A.why: You latched onto the first sentence. The counting method is only the starting point the narrator moves away from. The text never lays out a procedure, and the change in her view is the point.

C.why: You read a personal change of perspective as a recommendation. The narrator says she could no longer see the fish as numbers, but she never says counting is unreliable or should stop. Find the words that support a choice before you pick it.

D.why: You took the "mill" image too literally and made it sound destructive. The fish grinds a dead branch, not living coral, and the sand builds the shore rather than being lost. The text presents the fish as a maker, not a threat.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomás Reyes's 2021 memoir of his career as a bridge inspector.

My father, who built houses, trusted what he could see: a straight beam, a level floor. On my first inspection I found a bridge that looked flawless from the riverbank, its paint fresh and its railings true. Yet my sounding hammer rang dull over a hollow pocket in the concrete deck. I learned that day that a structure can keep its face long after it has lost its nerve.
choices: To contrast the narrator's career with his father's in order to express regret about leaving house building
To explain how inspectors use a sounding hammer to measure the thickness of a concrete deck
To recount an experience that taught the narrator a structure's appearance can hide its real condition
To show that the narrator's father taught him to rely on tools rather than on what he could see
explanation: The father "trusted what he could see." The bridge looks flawless, but the hammer finds a hollow inside it. The last sentence states the lesson in figurative terms: a structure can "keep its face" (look fine) after it has "lost its nerve" (become unsound). The text's purpose is to recount the experience that taught him this, which is C.

A.why: The text does set the narrator's lesson against his father's habit, but you added a feeling it never shows. Nothing suggests the narrator regrets his career or ever built houses himself.

B.why: You treated a detail as the subject. The hammer is how the narrator finds the hollow, but the text doesn't explain how the tool works or say it measures thickness. It is about what the moment taught him.

D.why: You reversed the father's role. He "trusted what he could see," which is the very view the narrator's experience calls into question. He did not teach the narrator to rely on tools.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Lindqvist's 2015 memoir about her work as a nutrition researcher.

In graduate school I believed a food was simply the sum of its label: so many grams of fiber, so many of sugar. Then our lab fed two groups identical portions of the same apples, one served whole and one pureed. The pureed group grew hungry again within the hour. A label, I realized, could describe a meal without describing what that meal would do.
choices: To argue that pureed fruit should be removed from diets because it causes hunger to return quickly
To explain that whole apples contain more fiber and less sugar than the same apples once pureed
To describe the daily routine the narrator followed while working in a graduate research laboratory
To describe how a study led the narrator to doubt that a food's listed nutrients fully predict its effects
explanation: The text follows an old belief, then a correction. The narrator first believed a food was "simply the sum of its label." A study then gave two groups identical apples, and only the preparation differed, yet the groups grew hungry at different times. Her conclusion is that a label can describe a meal "without describing what that meal would do." The purpose is to show how the study changed her belief, which is D.

A.why: You turned one result into a dietary recommendation. The narrator draws a lesson about labels, not advice about what people should eat. Nothing in the text says pureed fruit should be removed from anyone's diet.

B.why: The groups ate "identical portions of the same apples," so their labels would read the same. That sameness is what makes the result surprising. A difference in nutrients would undo the narrator's point.

C.why: You pictured a setting the text barely touches. The lab appears only as the place where one study happened. The text describes no routine, only the experiment that changed the narrator's thinking.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 2014 memoir by a former textile worker.

At the Harlan mill my mother was paid by the bolt, and she wove as if the loom owed her money. My aunt, hired that same spring at the dye works across the river, drew a flat weekly wage, and she kept pace with the slowest woman on her bench. By December the two had earned nearly the same amount, yet only my mother came home too tired to eat.
choices: To contrast how two different pay arrangements shaped the effort each woman gave to her work
To describe a conversation in which the mother and aunt compared the wages they had earned
To argue that workers paid by the bolt earn more over a year than workers paid a flat wage
To explain the steps by which cloth was woven at the mill and then colored at the dye works
explanation: Read the sentences as a pair: the mother is paid by the bolt and works furiously, while the aunt is paid a flat wage and works at the slowest pace. The last sentence sharpens the gap: they earned about the same, but only one was exhausted. The text exists to set those two arrangements side by side and show how each changed the effort put in.

B.why: You supplied a scene the text never shows. The narrator compares the two women, but nothing shows the women talking about their wages. Check that you can point to the words before you choose.

C.why: You assumed that harder work meant more pay. The text says the opposite: by December the two had earned nearly the same amount. That is the whole point of the comparison.

D.why: You latched onto the setting. The mill and the dye works are where the women work, but the text never describes how cloth is made. It is about how they were paid and how hard they worked.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from a 2003 novel. Inés, a graduate student in folklore, is recording her grandfather's stories.

Inés had arrived with a page of questions about the river spirit, and her grandfather answered none of them. Instead he told the story of the night the bridge washed out, and each time he reached the moment the lantern went dark, he stopped and looked at her tape recorder. To suggest that the grandfather will share the whole story but not let all of it be recorded

C.why: You invented content. The text mentions that Inés had a page of questions but never tells you what any of them were, so it cannot be listing them.

D.why: You took the story-within-the-story as the main subject. The bridge and the lantern are the material he tells, but the text never gives a time or place for that night. Its focus is on what he refuses to let the recorder capture.

For twenty years Okafor had trusted the alloy the way her father had trusted the harvest weather: it bent, it sprang back, it held. stem: Which choice does NOT describe a function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ruth Calder's 2009 memoir Leaves in Stone.

My father split shale the way other men read the morning paper: quickly, and every day. Most slabs held nothing, and he tossed them onto a pile by the shed without a second look. <u>But when a fern frond appeared, pressed flat and brown as weak tea, he would set the hammer down and stay still for a long time.</u> I learned early that he saved his patience for rare things.
choices: It sets his response to a fossil fern apart from his treatment of empty slabs.
It gives an example of the patience mentioned in the final sentence.
It suggests that a fossil meant more to him than an ordinary rock did.
It shows that he resented the hours he spent splitting shale each day.
explanation: Read the sentences on either side of the underlined line. The line before shows him tossing empty slabs aside, and the line after names his 'patience for rare things.' So the underlined sentence contrasts two reactions, illustrates that patience, and shows that a fern mattered to him. Nothing in the text shows resentment. Comparing his habit to reading the morning paper makes it sound routine, even comfortable. Choice D invents a feeling you can't point to in the text, so it is the one that fails.

A.why: This one is true. 'But' sets the stillness over the fern against the quick tossing of empty slabs in the sentence before. If you picked it, you probably stopped at the word 'sets apart' without checking it against the text. The question asks which choice is NOT a function.

B.why: This one is true. The final sentence names his patience, and the long stillness over the fern is the example of it. You may have thought the sentence and the final line were unrelated, but the final line is the general statement and the underlined sentence is the case that illustrates it.

C.why: This one is true, though not stated outright. You probably read the line too literally: he 'stays still', so you decided it says nothing about meaning. But a man who throws ordinary slabs away and stops for a fern is showing that the fern matters to him. The text supports this reading. It doesn't go beyond it.

stem: Which choice does NOT describe a function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Ilves's 2017 novel The Annealing Room.

Mira tested her glass by heating it and cooling it fast, then counting the cracks. Her colleague Dev left his samples in the oven overnight, letting them cool a degree at a time. <u>Mira's samples had shattered by noon; Dev's, set out the next morning, rang like bells when he tapped them.</u> Without saying a word to him, she began to slow down.
choices: It contrasts the outcomes of the two researchers' different methods.
It recounts a talk in which Dev explains his cooling method to Mira.
It uses a sound to suggest that Dev's glass had held together.
It prepares for the change Mira makes in the final sentence.
explanation: The underlined sentence sets Mira's shattered samples against Dev's intact ones. The image of glass ringing like a bell tells you his samples came through whole, and that result explains why Mira slows down in the next sentence. No conversation takes place anywhere in the text. The final sentence even says she changed 'without saying a word to him.' Choice B invents a talk you can't point to, so it is the one that fails.

A.why: This one is true. The semicolon divides the sentence into Mira's result and Dev's result, so the sentence does contrast the two methods. If you picked it, you probably found the sentence's subject and didn't check whether the choice was accurate. You're looking for the choice that is NOT a function.

C.why: This one is true. You probably read 'rang like bells' as a literal sound and decided that saying the glass 'held together' goes beyond the text. Cracked glass doesn't ring, though. The image is there to show that Dev's samples were sound, and set beside Mira's shattered ones, that is its point.

D.why: This one is true. Mira slows down because she has seen the two results side by side. You may have treated the last sentence as unconnected, but it is her response to what the underlined sentence shows.

stimulus:
The following text is from Ana Okafor's 2021 memoir Desire Lines.

When the city rebuilt our neighborhood park, the planners laid out neat walkways that crossed diagonally from corner to corner. Within a month, a brown stripe of trampled grass ran straight from the bus stop to the school gate. <u>Nobody had voted for that path, yet everyone had made it.</u> The following spring, the city poured concrete along it.
choices: It presents the worn path as a choice that residents made together.
It comments on how the stripe in the previous sentence came to exist.
It describes objections that residents raised at a city meeting.
It contrasts the lack of a formal decision with the path's wide use.
explanation: The underlined sentence looks back at the trampled stripe and explains how it formed: no one decided on it, but everyone's footsteps made it. The word 'voted' works figuratively and turns the path into a decision the residents made together without meaning to. The text never mentions a meeting or any objections. Residents walked, and then the city poured concrete. Choice C invents an event you can't point to, so it is the one that fails.

A.why: This one is true. You probably read 'nobody had voted' literally and decided that no choice was made, so calling the path a shared choice seemed unsupported. But 'everyone had made it' presents the path as a collective decision, made by walking rather than voting. That figurative reading is what the line is for.

B.why: This one is true. The sentence right before introduces the brown stripe, and 'that path' in the underlined sentence refers back to it and explains where it came from. You may have missed that 'that' links the two sentences.

D.why: This one is true. 'Nobody had voted' and 'everyone had made it' are set against each other with 'yet', which contrasts having no formal decision with heavy use. If you picked it, you probably found a choice that described the sentence and stopped without remembering that the question asks for the one that does NOT.
